title: Balaam's First Two Oracles: God Does Not Change His Mind
summary: Balak builds seven altars and offers sacrifices, hoping Balaam will curse Israel, but God puts a message in Balaam's mouth and he blesses them instead. Balak moves him to a second vantage point on Pisgah, and again Balaam blesses, declaring that God is not a man that he should lie and that no spell or divination can work against Israel. Frustrated, Balak takes him to a third place, the top of Peor.
story: The previous chapter ended with Balak taking Balaam up to a height where he could see the edge of Israel's camp. Now the contest begins. Balak thinks that with the right sacrifices and the right angle, Balaam can make a curse stick. Three times in chapters 23 and 24 he moves the seer to a new place and repeats the ritual, and each time the result is a blessing. This chapter contains the first two of Balaam's four oracles. Israel, camped below, knows nothing of what is being said about them; the reader overhears God defending his people against an attack they never saw. The oracles recall the promises to Abraham and Jacob and restate them for the generation about to enter the land.
historical:
The setting is the highlands of Moab overlooking the Jordan Valley, where Israel is encamped on the plains below. The places named, Bamoth-baal (22:41), the field of Zophim on the top of Pisgah (verse 14), and the top of Peor (verse 28), are heights on the edge of the plateau. Pisgah is the same range from which Moses will later view the land before he dies (Deuteronomy 34:1), and Peor will be the site of Israel's sin in chapter 25. Their exact locations are uncertain, but the idea is clear: Balak is looking for a better view, as though a curse needed a line of sight.

Balaam says he came from Aram and from the mountains of the east (verse 7), which fits the location of Pethor near the Euphrates in the previous chapter. Aram was the region of Syria and upper Mesopotamia, the homeland of Abraham's relatives (Genesis 24:10; 28:5). There is a fitting irony in a seer coming from the land of Israel's ancestors to curse Israel and ending up blessing them.
cultural:
Seven altars with a bull and a ram on each was an impressive and costly ritual. In the ancient Near East, sacrifices were offered before seeking an omen, and diviners often looked for signs in the organs of sacrificed animals or in natural events. Balaam's going off alone to a barren height (verse 3) to meet God fits that background, as does Balak's hope that a new place might produce a different result (verse 27). Balak assumes that the gods can be persuaded or maneuvered by ritual technique. The oracles overturn that assumption: “there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel” (verse 23).

An oracle (mashal) was a formal poetic pronouncement. The same word can mean a proverb, a taunt, or a parable, but in the Balaam chapters it names inspired speech in poetic lines. The images come from the world of the herder and the hunter: the wild ox, one of the strongest animals known, and the lioness and lion, which stand for Israel's strength. The shout of the King (verse 21) is a battle cry or a royal acclamation, the cheer that went up for a king among his troops.
literary: Each oracle follows the same frame: Balak builds altars, Balaam withdraws, God meets him and puts a word in his mouth, Balaam returns and speaks, and Balak objects. The repetition builds comedy and tension together, and Balak's reactions grow more desperate: first a complaint (verse 11), then a new location (verse 13), then a demand that Balaam neither curse nor bless (verse 25). The oracles themselves are Hebrew poetry, built on parallel lines in which the second restates or develops the first, such as “How can I curse what God has not cursed? How can I denounce what the LORD has not denounced?” Jacob and Israel are paired throughout as two names for the same people. The first oracle focuses on Israel's distinctness and numbers; the second on God's unchanging word and presence among them.

outline.t: The first oracle: a people dwelling apart
Balak's complaint and the move to Pisgah
The second oracle: God is not a man that he should lie
Balak's frustration and the move to Peor

doctrines.note: Verse 19 is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of God's faithfulness and truthfulness: he does not lie or change his mind like a human being, and what he promises he fulfills.

The oracles restate the covenant promises: descendants beyond counting like the dust (compare Genesis 13:16 and 28:14), God's presence with his people, and deliverance from Egypt. God's blessing on Israel is grounded in his commitment, not in their performance in the wilderness.
No ritual, sacrifice, or technique can force God's hand. The repeated failure of Balak's efforts shows that blessing and curse are God's decisions alone.

words.note: Mashal, oracle, proverb, or parable. It describes a formal, poetic saying. In the Balaam chapters it introduces each of his pronouncements, marking them as solemn speech, and the same word gives the book of Proverbs its Hebrew title.
Qavav, to curse or execrate. It appears repeatedly in Balak's demands. Balaam's reply in verse 8 turns the verb against itself: he cannot curse what God has not cursed.

Nacham, to relent or change one's mind. Verse 19 says God does not do this as humans do. Elsewhere the same verb is used when God relents from a threatened judgment (Exodus 32:14; Jonah 3:10), a tension discussed below.

Teru'ah, a shout or blast, used for battle cries, the trumpet blasts of festivals, and royal acclamation. The shout of the King among them (verse 21) pictures God as Israel's king present in their camp.

christ: The second oracle calls God the King among his people (verse 21), an early statement of the theme of God's kingship that grows through the Old Testament and reaches its fulfillment when Jesus announces the kingdom of God. The confession of verse 19, that God does not lie and always fulfills what he promises, is the ground of the New Testament's claim that all of God's promises find their yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). Balaam's wish to die the death of the righteous (verse 10) is poignant because he did not; Numbers 31:8 records that he was killed with the sword among Israel's enemies. The Bible's answer to that longing is not better religious technique but the righteousness God gives, which the New Testament locates in Christ. These are thematic links rather than predictions; the oracle that speaks more directly of a coming ruler comes in the next chapter.

hard.q: If God does not change his mind (verse 19), why do other passages say that he relented?
hard.a:
The Hebrew verb nacham is used both ways. Verse 19 says God is not a man that he should change his mind, and 1 Samuel 15:29 says something similar. Yet Exodus 32:14, Jeremiah 18:7-10, and Jonah 3:10 say that God relented from a judgment he had announced. Interpreters handle this in several ways. The classical view holds that God's nature and purposes never change, and that passages describing him relenting speak from the human point of view, describing a change in his dealings as people change. Others emphasize that God's warnings are often conditional by design (Jeremiah 18 says so explicitly), so relenting when people repent is part of his unchanging character rather than a change in it. Some contemporary theologians go further and argue that God truly responds and adapts in relationship with his creatures, a view others strongly resist.

The context of Numbers 23 is the key. Balak wanted God to be like a human king who could be bribed or persuaded to reverse a promise. Verse 19 denies that: God does not break his word under pressure. That claim is compatible with a God who is merciful when people repent, which the other passages show.

questions: Balak kept changing locations, hoping for a different answer from God. In what ways do people try to manage or maneuver God rather than listen to him?
Israel had no idea that a curse was being attempted against them, or that God was turning it into blessing. What comfort is there in knowing God may be protecting you in ways you never see?
Verse 19 says God does not lie and always fulfills what he promises. Which of his promises do you find hardest to believe right now?
